stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、macOS 15.8.2アップデートがOpenGLを壊したという報告と、それに伴うAppleのソフトウェア品質低下への懸念だ。多くのコメントでは、Appleが2018年にOpenGLを非推奨宣言して以来、奇跡的に動き続けていたが、今回のアップデートで最終的に機能が断たれたことを指摘し、これが「千枚の紙切れ」的な小さな不具合の積み重ねだと嘆く声が目立つ。一方で、OpenGLの代替としてLunarGのVulkan‑on‑MetalラッパーがVulkan 1.4に適合したことや、MesaのZink（OpenGL‑on‑Vulkan）が本番利用可能になる期待を示す前向きな意見もあり、賛否は「Appleの方針に従うべきか、クロスプラットフォームAPIの維持を求めるべきか」で分かれた。特に注目されたコメントは、OpenGLの非推奨宣言はAppleのシステムだから仕方がないとしつつ、それでも「私たちが期待するサポートはない」と現実的に受け止める姿勢を示したもので、今後のグラフィックスタックの移行路線について具体的な代替案を提示した点が評価された。
stories.editor_note: 最新のmacOSアップデートでOpenGLサポートが削除され、レガシーグラフィックアプリやゲームの動作が不安定になり、Metalへの移行が急がれる中、日本のゲーム開発者も影響を受けやすい状況が指摘されている。

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、ソフトウェアは作り手の「心」としての概念と、実際の製品がユーザーとの相互作用で完成するというアイデア、そして現代の開発組織が個々の変更を積み重ねる「フランケンシュタインの怪物」になる傾向、すなわちビジョンや責任が散らかっていることが指摘された点です。賛否両論として、一部はこの分析に共感し、職人気質のコードや設計を称賛する一方で、他は市場での成功例（JIRAなど）を挙げて、品質よりも商業的要因が優先される現実を指摘し、理想と実務のギャップを論じました。注目コメントでは、「各変更は独立して妥当でも、全体としては共有ビジョンがないと製品が歪む」という組織図の指摘や、「手作りのソフトウェアは技術書に残る職人技の残滓であり、もう一度復活させるべきだ」という職人精神への呼びかけが特に洞察に満ちていたと紹介されました。

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点  
Javaのsealed classesとexhaustive pattern matching（再帰パターンやリテラルパターン例 `switch (x) { case A(B(true, var c)) -> f(c); }`）の導入について、ScalaやKotlinとの機能比較が中心となり、言語の関数型志向が議論された。

・賛否両論  
賛成側は、パターンマッチングがコードの安全性と可読性を向上させ、Javaが最終的にモダンな言語機能に追いついたと評価。一方、懐疑的・否定的な意見は、Scalaの「indiscriminate」な複雑さの失敗例を挙げて、Javaが余計に難解になる危惧や、Kotlinがすでに洗練されているためわざわざ戻る理由がないと指摘した。

・注目コメント  
「Scala punching the air rn」というコメントは、Scalaが再び注目を集めている様子を皮肉りつつ期待を示しており、「Java continues to try and catch up to Kotlin」という指摘は、Javaの進化が他言語に追いつくための必死の努力だと洞察的に評価されている。
stories.editor_note: Java 21以降で強化されたsealedクラスとパターンマッチングは、状態安全なコードを書きやすくし、Androidアプリ開発でも採用が進むことで、日本のモバイルエンジニアに新たな設計パターンを提供している。

stories.summary_ja:

コミュニティでは、DeepSeekの有料検索API（1000リクエストあたり0.75ドル）のコストパフォーマンスが話題となり、自前でsearxng‑ai‑kitやoh‑my‑piなどのオープンソーススクレイパーを使えば無料で同等の結果が得られると指摘されている。また、これらのサービスが存在する理由として、Googleが有料検索APIを提供していないことが挙げられた。

・注目コメント  
一ユーザーは「CloudflareのチェックボックスやAnubisによる保護ページにアクセスしたとき、実際に欲しいコンテンツが取得できるのか、エラーや空レスポンスになるのか」と疑問を呈し、アンチボット対策の実効性が懸念点として挙げられた。また、別のコメントではKagiの10ドル/月プランは無制限だがLLMでの利用は利用規約違反だと指摘され、API利用時のライセンス注意が話題となった。

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点：記事の著者が次の8087チップのどの部分を取り上げるべきか読者に意見を求めている点。この質問は、記事シリーズの続編をどのように方向付けるかをコミュニティに問うもので、過去の記事では浮動小数点加減算のアルゴリズムが中心だったため、次はどの機能を掘り下げるべきかが焦点となっている。コメントは「次の記事でどのトピックを扱うべきか？」という単純な質問であり、スレッド全体がこの質問に集中している。  
・賛否両論：具体的な賛否や対立する意見は見られず、すべての参加者が著者の問いに答える形で提案をしているため、論争はない。ただし、いくつかのコメントでは乗算ユニットの詳細を求める声と、超越関数（sine、cosine、指数）の実装方法を解説してほしいという声が分かれており、興味の対象がやや異なることがうかがえる。  
・注目コメント：著者自身のこの問いかけが最も目立ち、読者からは「浮動小数点乗算」「例外処理」「マイクロコードの詳細」「命令セットの拡張」など様々な提案が寄せられ、特に「マイクロコード内部の状態機械」への関心が高いことを示している。あるユーザーは状態機械のフローチャートを図示してほしいと具体的に要望し、別のユーザーは8087の例外フラグの挙動を徹底的に解説してほしいとコメントしており、これらの提案が次回記事の有力な候補となっている。
stories.editor_note: 1980年代の数学コプロセッサーが浮動小数点演算を高速化した歴史的意義が再評価され、組み込み系やレトロコンピューティングの愛好家の中で日本でも関心が高まっている。

comments.author: BoppreH
comments.text: If you're on Python and your problem is too big for a single regex, but too small for a full-blown parser like in the article, I can recommend the built-in re.Scanner[0]. It's a regex-based tokenizer[1] (so no recursive parsing) in the `re` module, that for reasons is completely missing from any official documentation. You give it a pattern for each token type, and a function to process each match, and you get back a list of processed tokens. Importantly, it processes the list in one pass and ensures the matches are contiguous, where a naive `re.findall` with capture groups will ignore unmatched characters. You also get a reference to the running scanner, so you can record the location of the match for reporting errors. import re # Initialize the scanner. scanner = re.Scanner([ (r"\d+", lambda scanner, token: ('COUNT', int(token))), (r"\w+", lambda scanner, token: ('ANIMAL', token.removesuffix('s'))), (r"[,. ]", None), # None -> skip token. ]) # Scan a sample string. results, remainder = scanner.scan("45 pigeons, 23 cows, 11 spiders.") # Ensure we parsed the whole thing. assert not remainder print(results) # [('COUNT', 45), # ('ANIMAL', 'pigeon'), # ('COUNT', 23), # ('ANIMAL', 'cow'), # ('COUNT', 11), # ('ANIMAL', 'spider')] [0]: https://stackoverflow.com/a/693818/252218 [1]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexical_analysis#Tokenization

comments.author: ArneCode
comments.text: I really like the animations, makes it intuitive to understand what is happening! One disadvantage that I think parser combinators have, for example compared to parser generator libraries (where the parser is generated from a seperate grammar file), is that you have to add a lot of mapping / unwrapping code. In my opinion this makes the parsers harder to read. As an attempt to improve this, I have been working on a parser combinator library in rust. It adds two extra combinators (capture and bind) which can store the results of parsers in buckets (bind) and use the values stored in these buckets later to construct results (capture). This allows you to eliminate the unwrapping / mapping code and seperate the grammar from the result contstruction. If you have the time, I would really appreciate feedback on this! You can find it here: https://github.com/ArneCode/marser

comments.author: skew-aberration
comments.text: Coral gets its color from algae called zooxanthellae, which it depends on for photosynthesis. Bleaching is actually due to the coral expelling those algae. Bleached corals are not dead, and remarkably they can not only let the algae in again but can also select a different algae species to cultivate (changing colour in the process)!. This is thought to be a deliberate survival strategy to optimize the species of algae under different conditions (Adaptive Bleaching Hypothesis). Bleaching is caused by the same stressors (like high temperature) which kill coral, but bleaching itself is not death of the coral.

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**  
Teal の実用例として Luarocks のソースコードが挙げられ、実際に大規模コードベースで採用されていることが注目された。さらに、Algernon ウェブサーバーが組み込みで Teal をサポートしている点や、Luau との比較についての関心も示された。また、Teal の開発者の中心人物である Hisham（GoboLinux、htop の作者）の経歴が言及され、Lua 自体が「軽すぎる」という評価と、言語拡張の必要性について議論が交わされた。

**賛否両論**  
賛成側は、型付けによる安全性向上と大規模プロジェクトへの適用可能性を評価し、Luarocks や Algernon の事例を成功例として挙げた。一方、批判側は Lua のシンプルさが魅力であり、型システムを導入すると言語の軽快さが損なわれると指摘し、こうした実験が「芸術的」目的以外に意味があるのか疑問を呈した。

**注目コメント**  
「Lua は本当に軽い言語だと思う。構文も機能も最小限で、それで十分だと思っている」という意見が特に目を引いた。このコメントは、言語設計における「必要十分」のバランスについて考えさせられ、型付け拡張の実際のニーズとユーザーの期待値の違いを浮き彫りにした。
stories.editor_note: Luaに静的型付けを加えたTealが登場し、スクリプト言語でも型安全性を確保しやすくなり、日本のゲーム開発現場でのLua利用拡大に伴って導入検討が進んでいる。

The sentence is maybe ambiguous, but it sounds like it's saying to not use the AI at all until you understand what's happening in the area that needs to change. If at this point there is anything that is unclear to me about its approach to implement the plan, or I don't already have familiarity with the part of the system it's proposing to update, I start questioning the AI on how the system works. I will scrutinize the AI's plan until I'm absolutely sure that it's going to implement something that is sound from a system design perspective and as a senior software developer with architecture level experience I am capable of making such judgments. I'm not sure what it might be like for comparitively inexperienced developers, but I would expect that AI's capacity for infinite patience allows them to ask as many questions as they need to get a clear mental model of what's happening, so if I were mentoring such a person in this age of AI I would drill into them on how to interact with AIs to ensure they have this clarity before the AI starts implementing anything. comments.text: I get that Tao is a mathematician first and I respect the fact that he stays 'in his wheelhouse' (he didn't write the post but he did post it on his blog). But I think it would be fair to extrapolate and to wonder about this question not just for mathematics but for all of science. Keep in mind that scientific knowledge can be hoarded or used to patent stuff and that there is plenty of evidence that OpenAI, Anthropic and possibly others are going to go after other sources of income[1] than just selling access to their AI inference engines. I can imagine a future where these companies become the new Zaibatsus[2] holding patents across a wide variety of subject and with mutually re-inforcing silos of proprietary technology created by in-house AI that the rest of the world financed but does not have access to. comments.author: ttul
comments.text: My read on Terence Tao's comments of late is that professional mathematicians are principally upset about AI-submitted math papers lacking the kind of broad teaching content that high quality human math papers offer. While the answer might be correct, AI math papers don't teach the reader in the way a human author would have. Professional mathematics is not just about solving problems; it's just as much about spreading knowledge so that others can program their human brains with the same understanding that the paper's author had when they wrote the paper (and achieved the result). In other words, the crisis in mathematics (as I read it) is that AI can solve without teaching. The result may be impressive, but if the only beings that can move math forward in future are machines grinding away on billions of scenarios that no human would have the patience to undertake, this leaves those in the profession wondering about their place in it.

comments.author: itsalwaysgood
comments.text: These are all great points but I'd also point out that the 'dark age' scenario is a highly competitive scenario, while the 'golden age' scenario is a highly collaborative one. I don't think technology will fizzle out in either scenario. In the 'dark age' highly competitive scenario, you will still have those who 'understand what is produced' seeking progress and advancement. They will cohort with whoever/whichever organization is producing the best, most validated results. I don't think knowledge would be become alien to human understanding, it would just become highly concentrated again as it was in the past. In the past, only the wealthy and noble could afford to spend time on education. And usually, those who went deep into any field and provided contributions to science were those who had time to devote entire lives to the study or pursuit of knowledge. We still have these issues today, and these issues will always be present. There is a supply chain of economy, and we provide different rewards based on the value of what is produced. The jobs never go away, the desire for prestige, greed, etc., never goes away. It's why economies exist, and it's why everyone is considering the value of LLMs, and their place in economies, and academies (presumably which exist to advance human understanding/appreciation, but also to prepare younger generations for future work).

comments.author: odyssey7
comments.text: Obviously a golden age. I’m not bitter about this anymore — it’s been a long time. But the story holds something. Back in the day, I knew I was talented at mathematics, and I wanted to pursue a research career. For a freshman research class, I selected a problem that was intentionally outside my comfort zone, and came up with some cool ideas. It wasn’t publication quality, though the course wasn’t really expecting publications. Framing the problem in a way that it could be solved with calculus turned out to be a key insight. I turned to Wolfram, since the integrals were beyond what I as a freshman could have done myself, and I understood that the insight that produced the solution was my original work. I don’t think anyone in the class could have done those integrals. The instructor himself couldn’t tell me what was wrong with them if anything. Yet, he was unimpressed and subtly dismissive or critical. Today, I might have been in the wave of researchers developing AI for mathematics work. The instructor could have been proud of shaping mathematics through his mentorship. The university might have invited me for talks. Instead, I ended up leaving mathematics as a field altogether. Now, I write software for a bank. The world is as rich as we make it. Don’t let your opportunities and potential expire. Embrace the materials that are available to work with, or someone else will and they will out compete you and you will have missed the moment. I get that there’s a romantic idea of what mathematicians do, and the field changing creates a sort of identity crisis. I would argue that the field has entered a new era. Exploring and shaping this era of mathematics is the opportunity of a lifetime. Embrace it, drive it, and make your mark.

comments.author: nickysielicki
comments.text: Suppose lean in its current state existed 15 years ago, and suppose the math community eagerly started contributing en masse to a shared repository of code. How much of the breakthroughs and longstanding questions in mathematics that we’ve seen answered this year do you think we would have solved? In other words, how much of the developments this year are directly attributable to LLMs using lean, versus lean just being a significantly more productive language for some subset of mathematics compared to English and LaTeX? Given how much we’ve seen formalized this year it feels hard to believe that this couldn’t have happened earlier. Follow up question: do you think mathematicians would be as upset about the rapid changes in their field if they were the result of a collective shared effort on github, authored entirely by humans who all share the credit, versus that same outcome but authored by a large language model? In other words, are the mathematicians upset about large language models, or are they really just upset that formalization and massive collaboration have turned out to be highly effective and has negated the heroic angle that mathematicians previously enjoyed, thinking in a locked room by themselves? Food for thought. A coworker recently remarked that lean seems like a new foundational language family that every programmer should be able to read, on par with C and Python, and I think it’s pretty hard to disagree with that. Next generations of models are going to be RL’d on Lean more and more because it pays dividends in winning the math war against their competitors, and this will benefit users of lean not only for mathematics but also as a general programming language and as a vehicle for other DSLs. comments.author: TazeTSchnitzel
comments.text: I think this is a rare “useful” abuse of font ligatures, and in that respect I think this is a cool project, but it's also a terrible idea that nobody should actually use, because Japanese kanji readings are famously ambiguous and context-dependent. The modal character has two different readings without counting those used in personal names, nor contextual slight changes to pronunciation. Some characters have six different readings, and that's again without counting those used in personal names. There's no way a font can do a good job at it unless you can somehow stuff an entire LLM in there. For context, it's a hard enough problem that Google Translate's own romanised pronunciation guides are frequently wrong, or disagree with their text-to-speech.

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**: フォントのリガチュアで自動的にふりがなを表示する仕組みの実用性と限界について議論された。技術的にはクールで学習者支援になる可能性があるが、漢字の読みが文脈に強く依存し、多義性が高いため完全に正確なふりがな付与は困難という指摘が中心だった。  
**賛否両論**: 賛成側は「フォントだけでふりがなが出るのは画期的」「初学者や dyslexic 読者に助けになる」と称賛。一方で否定側は「読みが文脈によって変わるため誤りが多い」「リガチュアでは辞書登録されていない語や複合語が正しく処理されず、改行で分断されると誤ったふりがなが出る」と批判した。  
**注目コメント**: ネイティブスピーカーは「合字」が「ごうじ」と表示されず「じ」だけになる点を指摘し、辞書欠如によるフォールバックを説明。また、改行で大学が分断されると誤ったふりがなが出たと報告。さらに「この先生きのこるには」の例がネットミームから学習したように見えるとの観察や、完全な解析にはLLMが必要だという意見も挙げられた。
